title: Dasharatha's death and the curse that caused it (Shravana Kumara)
hook: a king dies at midnight, and a boy with no name in the oldest text becomes one of India's best-known sons

segments.voice: Yesterday: Dasharatha's death and the curse that, part two. The prince told the blind parents the truth, and the father said: you too will die grieving for a son. Did you say something straight yesterday? Day five hundred forty-four.
screen: `YOU TOO WILL GRIEVE FOR A SON.`

segments.voice: In many Indian homes, children hear about the young man at the river long before anyone reads them the Ramayana. In those tellings he has a name, Shravan Kumar, and a picture to go with it: a son carrying his blind parents on a pilgrimage, one in each of two baskets hung from a pole across his shoulders. Grandparents tell it at bedtime as the story of a good son. So here's a small surprise. In Valmiki's Ramayana, the young man doesn't have a name, and there are no baskets. Both came later.
screen: `A NAME CHILDREN KNOW.` → `TWO BASKETS ON A POLE.` → `IN VALMIKI, NO NAME.`

segments.voice: The night ends. Dasharatha finishes the story, and he knows what it means. The curse is arriving. He tells Kausalya his eyes are failing, that he can't see her anymore. He says, in effect, if only Rama would come back and touch me now. He names the people who are lucky enough to see Rama's face when he returns. And somewhere past midnight, still speaking of his son, the old king dies. In the morning, the singers and attendants come to wake him as they always do, and find him gone. The palace breaks into grief. And because no son is there to perform the last rites, Rama in the forest and Bharata far away in his grandfather's kingdom, the ministers do something unusual. They lay the king's body in a vessel of oil, to keep it until Bharata can be brought home. Messengers ride for Kekaya with strict orders: say nothing of what has happened. Just bring him. Now the name. Valmiki calls the boy simply the young ascetic, the hermit's son. Later retellings, in regional languages and folk tradition, call him Shravana, or Shravan Kumar, and they add the picture of the baskets and the pilgrimage. The name fits him oddly well. Shravana is a Sanskrit word connected with hearing, and this is a boy killed by an archer who shot at a sound. So the story grew, over the centuries, around the one detail Valmiki left open, and the boy who had no name became a byword for loving your parents.
screen: `THE KING DIES PAST MIDNIGHT.` · `A BODY KEPT IN OIL FOR BHARATA.` · `IN VALMIKI, THE HERMIT'S SON.` · `LATER: SHRAVAN KUMAR, AND THE BASKETS.` · then, large: `A NAME THAT GREW.`

segments.voice: Sit and let the body settle. Bring to mind someone older who looked after you: a parent, a grandparent, a teacher, a neighbor. If that's hard, choose anyone who once carried something for you. See their face. Notice one specific thing they did, a meal, a ride, a hand on your shoulder. Let your breath stay with that picture. If you pray, you can hold them in your prayer in your own way. The bell holds the time.
Shravana, hearing, the name later tellings give the boy at the river. Dasharatha dies grieving for his son, as that boy's father said he would.
Your line: riders for Kekaya. Today, call or message one older person who once carried something for you. Day five hundred forty-four.

howItsDone: Shravan Kumar is a common children's story across much of India, told to teach care for parents, and his name is still used as praise for a devoted son or daughter.

fork.setup: you're a minister. the king has died, and both sons who could perform the rites are far away. what do you do?
options: hold the funeral at once without them.
keep the body and send for Bharata.
send for Rama in the forest.

original.note: Sanskrit śravaṇa: hearing, listening. the name later tellings give the boy at the river.

trapdoor: what you thought: Shravan Kumar is a character in Valmiki's Ramayana.
what it means: Valmiki's boy is unnamed; the name and the baskets grew up in later retellings.
what a scholar hears: Valmiki's young ascetic is a muni's son; the pilgrimage with the carrying pole belongs to later regional and folk tradition.

notes: Confirm the boy is unnamed in Valmiki (critical edition and vulgate); the script says so plainly.

'Shravana is connected with hearing' is offered as a fitting coincidence, not an etymology for the story; confirm the tone is acceptable.
